title: What is price elasticity, and how do you use it in a pricing case?
description: Price elasticity explained simply, with a worked example of whether a price rise increases revenue and profit, and how to talk about it in a case.
hook: Price elasticity is the percentage change in volume divided by the percentage change in price, and in a pricing case it tells you whether a price change will raise or lower profit. The most useful way to apply it is to work out how much volume the client can afford to lose (or must gain) for the price change to pay off, then judge whether real customers would behave that way.
body:
The idea

Elasticity = % change in volume ÷ % change in price. It is usually negative, because a higher price means fewer sales.

  • If a 10% price rise loses 5% of volume, elasticity is −0.5. Demand is inelastic: customers are not very sensitive to price.
  • If a 10% rise loses 20% of volume, elasticity is −2. Demand is elastic: customers are very sensitive.

The dividing line is −1. When demand is inelastic, a price rise increases revenue; when it is elastic, a price rise reduces revenue. But revenue is not profit, and in a case it is profit that usually matters.

A worked example

A product sells 100,000 units a year at $10, with a variable cost of $6 a unit. Revenue is $1M and contribution is 100,000 × $4 = $400k. The client is considering a 10% price rise to $11, which lifts contribution per unit to $5.

Volume changeElasticityRevenueContribution
Nown/a$1,000k$400k
−5% (95,000)−0.5$1,045k$475k
−10% (90,000)−1.0$990k$450k
−20% (80,000)−2.0$880k$400k

Look at the middle row. At an elasticity of −1, revenue falls slightly, yet contribution rises by $50k, because the units lost were each costing $6 to make. A candidate who only looks at revenue would reject a price rise that makes the client more money.

The break-even volume change

The question to answer in almost every pricing case is: how much volume can we lose before the price rise stops paying?

Keep contribution at $400k with $5 per unit: $400k ÷ $5 = 80,000 units, a 20% fall. As a shortcut:

  • Price rise: maximum volume loss = price increase ÷ (old unit contribution + price increase) = $1 ÷ ($4 + $1) = 20%.
  • Price cut: volume gain needed = price cut ÷ (old unit contribution − price cut). Cutting to $9 gives $1 ÷ ($4 − $1) = 33%. The client would need to sell 133,333 units just to stand still.

Notice the asymmetry: a 10% cut needs a 33% volume gain, while a 10% rise can survive a 20% loss. Note too that the thinner the margin, the more volume a price rise can afford to lose. With $9 of contribution on a $10 product, a $1 rise could only lose 10% of volume before it stopped paying; with $1 of contribution, it could lose 50%. Break-even volume uses the same logic.

What affects elasticity

  • Close substitutes make demand more sensitive.
  • Essentials and habits make it less sensitive.
  • Share of the customer's budget: people notice price rises on big purchases more than on small ones.
  • Switching costs and contracts reduce sensitivity in the short term.
  • Time: demand is often less elastic in the short run than the long run, as customers take time to find alternatives.
  • Competitor response: if rivals match the price rise, the client loses far fewer customers than if they hold their prices.

Elasticity also varies by customer group and price point. An estimate from a past 3% price change may not hold for a 20% one. If the client has the data, look at past price changes by segment, or test a limited change in one region. The three ways to set a price puts this into a wider pricing structure.

How to say it

Strong: "A 10% price rise pays off as long as we lose fewer than 20% of units. With few close substitutes and annual contracts, I'd expect a much smaller loss, so it looks attractive. I'd test it in one region first and watch whether competitors follow."
Weak: "If we raise prices, we'll lose some customers, so revenue might go down. It depends on elasticity."

Common mistakes

  • Judging on revenue, not profit. Lost units also save variable cost.
  • Getting the ratio upside down. Volume change goes on top, price change underneath.
  • Assuming one elasticity fits every price change and every customer.
  • Ignoring competitors. Their reaction can matter more than customers' first response.

Practice

1. A 5% price rise cuts volume by 15%. What is the elasticity, and what happens to revenue?

Show the answer

−15% ÷ 5% = −3, so demand is elastic. Revenue falls: 1.05 × 0.85 = 0.89, a drop of about 11%.

2. Price is $50 and variable cost $30. How much volume can the client lose if it raises the price to $55?

Show the answer

$5 ÷ ($20 + $5) = 20%. Check with 100 units: now 100 × $20 = $2,000; after, 80 × $25 = $2,000.

3. Same product: what volume gain does a cut to $45 need?

Show the answer

$5 ÷ ($20 − $5) = 33%. Check: 100 × $20 = $2,000; 133.3 × $15 = $2,000.
